body.text:
My best friend got very handsy with the man I'd loved for over fifty years.
A widow at sixty-four, with butterflies she meant to take.
She was welcome to try.

Tom was a good man. The best I ever knew.

Forty years we had. I'd have taken forty more.

Near the end, when we both knew, he took my hand and made me promise him something.

"Don't shut yourself away when I'm gone, Carol. You were made for loving. Don't you dare stop."

I promised. I just didn't believe I'd ever want to.

I lost him four years ago.

And grief isn't the hard part. You see grief coming.

It's the quiet that gets you.

The cold half of the bed you stop reaching across.

Cooking for one. Eating at the counter, because the table feels too big now.

The good perfume going to dust on the shelf, because who's it for.

Some weeks nobody touched me at all. Not a hand on my arm. Nothing.

You don't die of that. You just forget you were ever a woman somebody reached for.

The kids call. The grandkids call. Most days it's enough.

Most days.

The one who still came round was Gloria.

We'd been friends thirty years. The kind you keep out of habit, not love.

Widowed, like me. But where it made me go quiet, it made her go hungry.

I told myself that was just Gloria.

Then one ordinary Tuesday, Facebook put a name at the top of my screen.

People you may know, it said.

A name I hadn't seen in over fifty years.

I had to sit down.

Because there'd been a boy once. When I was twelve.

He lived next door. One afternoon he kissed me behind his father's car, where the grown-ups couldn't see.

Then his family moved away. And that was that.

For fifty years, that was that.

And now here was his name, looking back at me.

Danny.

The years had done their work. But the eyes in that little photo hadn't changed at all.

So I wrote to him. Before I could talk myself out of it.

"This will sound mad. Did you once live on Maple Street? The white house, green door?"

He answered in four minutes.

"Took me an hour to place you. Carol. The girl from the driveway."

Fifty years, and he remembered the driveway.

We dug out the old photos. And there we were.

Me on the left, gap-toothed. Him beside me. Two kids squinting into the sun.

After that, we talked every single day.

Like teenagers. Exactly like teenagers.

My phone would chime and my stomach would flip. It hadn't done that since I was a girl.

The first time we video called, I changed my blouse twice.

Sixty-four years old, stood at my closet like it was prom.

His face filled the screen and we both went quiet.

Two old faces where two kids used to be.

Then he grinned that same grin, and fifty years fell away.

"You still chew your lip when you're nervous," he said.

Nobody had seen me like that in years.

He told me about the day his family drove off. How he pressed his hand to the back window until our street was gone.

I never knew he'd looked back.

Fifty years, and I never knew he'd looked back.

And one night, halfway through a message, I heard Tom. Clear as if he were in the room.

Don't you dare stop.

For the first time in four years, I didn't want to.

Then he asked me to Mexico.

He goes every winter with the same crowd of friends. The same coast, year after year.

This year, he wanted me there too.

A whole week. The boy from the driveway, taking me to the sea.

I said yes before my head could catch up with my mouth.

I was so happy I had to tell someone.

So I told Gloria.

I should have known better.

She poured the wine and let me get it all out. Danny, the photos, Tulum.

And I watched something go flat behind her eyes.

"Well," she said. "Aren't you the lucky one."

She set her glass down.

"Can I say something? As your friend?"

I should have said no.

"You're flying halfway round the world to throw yourself at a man you knew when you were twelve. At our age."

Then, softer. Which was worse.

"And between us girls. There's a thing that happens to women our age. Some of us get a... a strong smell. You'd be the last to know it yourself. But a man gets close, and, well. I'd hate for you to embarrass yourself."

She squeezed my arm and went for her coat.

Thirty years I'd called that woman my friend. I sat beside her the day she buried her husband.

And she waited until I was happy. Properly happy, for the first time in years. Just to reach in and switch off the light.

And just like that, the butterflies were gone.

I drove home with my face hot. I spent three nights with my thumb over the cancel button.

The dream was safe as long as I stayed home.

One more week of dreaming felt better than one ruined moment in his arms.

I almost called it off.

Instead, I went to my sister June.

When the world tips over, June is who I call. Always has been.

Thirty years a nurse. Nothing on this earth shocks her.

I told her all of it. Danny. Mexico. What Gloria said.

She didn't gasp. She didn't waste a breath on Gloria.

She got up, opened a drawer, and put a little bar on the table.

"Here. Take this. It's a persimmon bar called Kaori."

I looked at it. Didn't pick it up. "So she was right."

"She was cruel. That's not the same thing." June sat back down. "It's nothing to be ashamed of, love. It's just a fat the body makes as we get older. Something to do with the hormones. Almost every woman our age has it. Not one of them needs to lose sleep over it."

"Then why has no soap ever fixed it?"

"Because soap was never made for it. Ordinary soap is for sweat and dirt. This is an oil. The water slides right off it. So you scrub, you cover it with perfume, and it only gets louder."

"And persimmon doesn't?"

"Persimmon takes it away. Doesn't hide it. Lifts it clean off. The Japanese have used it for this longer than you and I have been alive. We sent half the ward home with a bar."

I still hadn't touched it.

"I can't, June. Taking it feels like saying she was right."

"Oh, give over." She closed my fingers around it. "Take it. You can be proud and clean at the same time."

So I took it.

"And order more while you can," she said. "They make it in small batches. This lot's nearly gone. Once it sells out, that's it for months."

I turned the little bar over in my hands.

And I heard Tom again. Clear as anything. Don't you dare stop.

I drove home and cancelled nothing. The ticket was mine.

Gloria could scheme. Gloria could whisper. Gloria could do her worst.

She was welcome to try.

I was getting on that plane.

I used it the next morning.

It left the faintest green smell on my skin. Like a garden after rain.

By the end of that first week, I caught myself at the mirror longer than I had in years.

Not fixing anything. Just standing. A little taller, somehow.

My skin felt different. Lighter.

For the first time in four years, I was getting ready for someone.

And the woman looking back wasn't a widow doing her best.

She looked like a girl with a secret.

He was waiting at the airport. He didn't see sixty-four.

"There she is," he said. "The girl from the driveway."

He pulled me into a hug right there at arrivals.

I'd forgotten what it was to be held by someone who meant it.

And then, over his shoulder, I saw her.

Gloria. A few feet back. Suitcase at her heel. Lipstick fresh. Smiling like she'd planned the whole thing.

Because she had.

Same week. Same coast. She'd had every detail out of me over that glass of wine, and used the lot.

"Carol!" she called, all sugar. "What a coincidence."

It was no coincidence.

She had followed me across an ocean. To the one week of my life I'd dared to want something for myself. And she was smiling about it.

She didn't waste her week.

By our second night, his friends had a table by the water. Music. Warm dark. Little lights strung over the sand.

And Gloria, of course, right in the thick of it.

By the time I came down, she'd pulled her chair against his. Laughing too loud. That fresh lipstick an inch from his ear.

Her hands were all over the man I'd loved for fifty years. His sleeve. His arm. His knee.

This was the moment she'd been counting on. The one where I hang back in the doorway and let her have him.

The old me might have.

But I'd left that woman at home.

So I didn't wait. I walked straight over.

"Evening, Gloria," I said. And I never once looked at the hand she had on his knee.

Then I turned to Danny and held out mine. "Dance with me."

He was on his feet before I'd finished asking. Like he'd been waiting all night to get out of that chair.

He stepped past Gloria like she was a coat stand.

A slow song was playing. He pulled me in close. Closer than anyone had been in years.

I braced for it. That old fear. Gloria's voice in my ear.

And it didn't come.

He breathed me in like a man who'd held his breath for fifty years.

"God," he said into my hair. "You smell like a garden."

The one thing Gloria swore would send him running. And it only pulled him closer.

"You even feel like home."

We swayed there a while. Not really dancing. Just holding on.

And right there, in front of everyone, in front of Gloria, I kissed him.

The second kiss of my life.

With the same boy who gave me the first.

Nobody looked away. A couple of them actually cheered.

The last I saw of Gloria that night, she was gathering her things from an empty table.

Gloria still rings now and then. I let it go to voicemail.

I'm selling the house. Danny's selling his too. We're heading south, the both of us. Where else but Mexico.

My sister rang the week I got home.

"Well?" was all she said. She could already hear the answer.

"I'll need more of that bar," I told her.

"Then order it tonight. Fresh batch, and it's already half gone. Once it sells out, you wait till next year." A pause. "And tell every woman you know. Especially the ones who've stopped getting held the way they used to."

I sat a while after we hung up.

I thought about Gloria's hand on his knee. And the empty table she left it at.

About three sleepless nights with my thumb over a cancel button.

About a promise I made a good man, and very nearly broke.

And about ten quiet minutes at a sink that handed me back a woman I thought was gone for good.

If someone you love has been quietly pulling away, and you can't work out why.

If a voice keeps telling you your best days, and your best kisses, are behind you.

Maybe you don't need to win the argument.

Maybe you just need a better bar.

It's called Kaori. The link's below, while there's still some in.

The girl from the driveway got her boy.

And fifty years on, the butterflies hadn't aged a day.

Japón resolvió esto hace décadas con un solo ingrediente ✅

Un cambio. 3 días. Tu familia nota la diferencia antes que tú 🔄

cards.body:
My ex-husband's girlfriend has known my daughter for five months. I've known her for 43 years. At her birthday, everybody realized who's the real mom.

Tom and I divorced a year ago. We were married for 44 years.

Five months ago, he started dating Alexandra. She's 56. I'm 67.

Our daughter Cayce is 43. She's been living in Valencia for two years, working as a curator at a contemporary art museum.

Cayce is quiet. Thoughtful. She's always been that way. She reads constantly. Draws in coffee shops. Lives in oversized sweaters and zero makeup. She hates flashy things. Hates showing off. Hates anything that screams "look at me."

Cayce used to fall asleep on my shoulder during movies. Used to grab my arm when we walked together. Used to press her face into my neck when she hugged me.

That stopped about two years ago.

I didn't notice at first. Then I noticed.

Last Christmas she flew home. Hugged me at the door. Quick. Polite. Pulled away fast. Sat across the room instead of next to me on the couch. I told myself she was jet-lagged.

The visit before that. Showing her something on my phone and she leaned away. Driving her to lunch and she opened the window even though it was cold outside.

Little things. But they kept adding up.

On FaceTime she's the same Cayce. Warm. Laughing. Tells me everything. But in person? Something shifts. She keeps her distance. Keeps it short. Last two visits she flew home for three days instead of a week.

When Tom told me about Alexandra, part of me thought: maybe that's it. Maybe Cayce just likes her better. Maybe a 56-year-old woman who wears nice clothes and goes to restaurants in Milan is easier to be around than a 67-year-old retired teacher who still uses the same purse she bought in 2014.

I didn't say that to anyone. But I thought it every night for a week.

When Cayce turned 43, she wanted both parents there. Tom said yes. Alexandra insisted on coming.

"I want to be there for Cayce's big day," she told Tom.

They'd known each other for five months.

A week before the trip, Tom called me.

"Hey, so... Alexandra already got Cayce's gift. From both of us. Just letting you know."

"What did she get her?"

"I don't know. She handled it. Said it's perfect."

Perfect. Alexandra had known my daughter for five months and decided she knew what "perfect" was.

I hung up.

I met my friend Elena for coffee the next day. Elena and I have been friends for forty years. I taught high school English for 31 years before I retired. Elena worked at the same school. Front office. She knows me better than anyone alive.

I told her about Valencia. About Cayce's birthday. About Alexandra buying the gift.

"What are you getting her?" Elena asked.

"First edition of 'To Kill a Mockingbird.' Cayce's been searching for one for years. I found it at an estate sale three months ago."

Elena's eyes went wide. "That's incredible. How much?"

"Three hundred dollars."

I stirred my coffee.

"I just hope she actually wants me there."

"What do you mean?"

"I don't know. She's different with me lately. Not cold, just... careful. Like she's keeping a little distance. At Christmas she barely sat near me. She hugged me when she walked in and then kind of... let go fast. Sat on the other side of the room."

"Since when?"

"Two years maybe? I keep telling myself it's nothing. She's busy. She lives in another country. But in person something's off. She keeps it short. Last two visits she came home for three days instead of a week."

Elena didn't say anything for a moment.

"And now Alexandra's coming to Valencia. Playing family. Buying gifts. And I'm sitting here wondering if my own daughter is going to hug me or just wave from across the restaurant."

Elena put her cup down.

"Madison, can I tell you something? And I need you to actually hear me before you react."

"What?"

"You're not losing Cayce. And she's not pulling away because of who you are. Not the way you think."

"Then why?"

Elena looked at me the way she looks at me when she's about to say something I don't want to hear. She's done it maybe four times in forty years.

"Do you remember my mother-in-law? How the kids always sat on the other end of the couch when we visited her?"

"Yeah."

"We thought it was just kids being kids. Turns out it wasn't."

"Elena, what are you talking about?"

"After about 60, your body starts producing something called nonenal."

"Nonenal?"

"It's a chemical. Comes through your skin. And it has a smell. Not like sweat. Not like you forgot deodorant. Something different. Kind of stale. Waxy. And the thing is, you can't smell it on yourself. Your own nose goes blind to it. But the people close to you, physically close, they notice."

I felt my face get hot.

"Your soap doesn't do anything about it. Neither does perfume. Perfume just sits on top."

"How do you know all this?"

"Because it happened to me. Two years ago. My sister-in-law is Japanese. She sat me down one weekend and told me. Over there they have a name for it. Kareishuu. She said it's not something anyone talks about here, but in Japan everyone knows. It's just what happens."

"And what, there's some magic fix?"

"Persimmon. Something in it actually kills nonenal. Doesn't just cover it. There's a soap my sister-in-law uses. Kaori. She gave me a bar and told me to just try it for a week."

"Did you?"

"I almost didn't. I was angry. I cried in the shower the first time I used it, honestly. But then about a week later my granddaughter climbed into my lap during a movie. She hadn't done that in a year. And my daughter stopped cracking the window in the kitchen every time I came over. Nobody said anything. It just... shifted back."

I didn't say anything for a while.

"Madison. You're about to fly to Spain to see a daughter who lives 5,000 miles away. A daughter you just told me barely sits near you anymore. Don't go there and wonder why."

I looked it up that night. Kaori Persimmon Soap.

I almost didn't order it. I sat there for an hour. Part of me wanted to believe Cayce was just busy. Just tired. Just growing up.

But the window in the car. The quick hug at Christmas. The couch.

I ordered it.

It arrived three days before Valencia.

I used it every shower. Morning and night. It didn't smell like perfume. Didn't smell like much of anything. Clean. Warm. Quiet.

Valencia was beautiful. Golden light everywhere.

We met Cayce at her apartment the first day. She hugged Tom. Nodded politely at Alexandra.

Then she hugged me.

And held on.

Three seconds. Four. Five.

She didn't pull away.

"Hi, Mom."

I almost cried right there.

The birthday dinner was on day three. A restaurant Cayce loved. Small. Quiet. Candles on every table.

Cayce's friends from the museum were there. Eight of us total.

Cayce sat next to me. Leaning in when she talked. The way she used to.

At one point during appetizers, Alexandra was telling a story about a restaurant in Milan. Cayce leaned over to me and whispered, "I'm so glad you're here."

Then she rested her head on my shoulder. Just for a second. Like she was 12 again.

Alexandra stopped mid-sentence. Watched.

After dinner, Cayce's roommate brought out a cake. Everyone sang.

Then came the gifts.

Tom looked at Alexandra. "Do you have it?"

"It's in the suitcase. Let me grab it."

She stood up. Walked to the corner where she'd left her silver Rimowa.

We all watched her unzip it. Dig through folded clothes. Pull out a box.

The Louis Vuitton box was destroyed.

Not just crushed. Flattened on one side. The corners completely caved in. The signature brown packaging torn at the edges. Someone had re-taped it with clear packing tape that didn't even cover the rips.

She walked back to the table holding it.

Set it down in front of Cayce.

Everyone stared.

"Sorry," Alexandra said quickly. "TSA opened my luggage. They must have... repacked it wrong."

Tom's jaw tightened. "Jesus, Alexandra."

"The bag inside is fine. I checked."

Alexandra opened the destroyed box. Tissue paper spilled out. She pulled out a mini Louis Vuitton bag. Cream leather. Gold chain. Monogram print.

She handed it to Cayce.

Cayce held it. Didn't smile.

"Do you like it?" Alexandra asked.

"It's... nice."

"It's the mini Pochette Accessoires. Everyone has them right now."

Cayce set it on the table. "Thank you."

The table went quiet.

Cayce doesn't wear designer bags. She carries a canvas tote from the museum gift shop.

I reached into my bag. Pulled out the wrapped package.

The corners sharp. The ribbon still tied.

I handed it to Cayce.

"Happy birthday."

She unwrapped it carefully.

When she saw the book, her hands froze.

"Mom."

She opened the cover. First edition. 1960. Harper Lee's signature on the title page.

Her eyes filled with tears.

"You found it."

"Three months ago."

She stood up. Hugged me hard. Pressed her face into my neck. Stayed there.

"You smell like home," she whispered.

I held her. And for the first time in two years, she didn't pull away.

One of her friends leaned over to look. "Wait. Is that signed?"

"First edition," I said.

Tom was staring at the book. "How much did that cost?"

"It doesn't matter."

Alexandra was staring at the destroyed Louis Vuitton box on the table. The mini bag sitting next to it. Untouched. Then she looked at Cayce, still pressed against my shoulder.

Tom looked at Alexandra. Then at me.

Five months versus 43 years.

Everyone at that table saw the difference.

When I got home from Valencia, Elena called.

"How was the birthday?"

"Perfect."

"And Alexandra?"

"Brought Cayce a Louis Vuitton bag. Mini Pochette. $800. Box showed up destroyed. TSA tore through her Rimowa."

Elena laughed. "And Cayce?"

"She said I smell like home."

Elena didn't say anything for a moment.

"I need to order more before I run out."

"Good luck. I tried to reorder last month. They were out of stock for three weeks. Small batches. Persimmon from Japan. When it's gone, it's gone."

"You're kidding."

"I'm not. I have my sister-in-law send me two bars at a time now."

I hung up and went straight to the site. Still in stock.

I ordered three bars.

I almost didn't order that first bar. I almost flew to Spain and sat across the restaurant from my own daughter and told myself she was just busy.

Kaori Persimmon Soap. Look it up.

cards.body:
I lost my granddaughter at 66 because I can't smell. She told her mom my house makes her sick. I can't smell a thing. But that I heard.

I was in the kitchen. She was in the hallway with her mom. She didn't know I was there.

"Mommy I don't want to go to grandma's house. It makes me sick."

My sweet girl. The one who used to fall asleep on my chest every Sunday. That girl just told her mother that being near me makes her sick.

I stood there holding the counter and I couldn't breathe. Makes her sick. What makes her sick? What is she talking about?

I lost my sense of smell a year before Covid hit. It never came back. Not even a little. I can't smell my food, my clothes, my house, my own skin. Nothing. So when my granddaughter says something makes her sick, I can't just sniff it out like a normal person. I'm blind.

That night I didn't sleep.

I crawled through every room on my hands and knees trying to understand what she meant. Pressed my face into the couch cushions. Nothing. Held my curtains against my nose. Nothing. Put my face flat on the carpet. Nothing.

What is it, baby? What are you smelling? I was begging my house to give me an answer my nose couldn't.

I cleaned everything. Every surface, every fabric, every corner. Had the pipes checked. Had someone look for mold. Opened every window for days in the middle of winter. None of it mattered. Because I couldn't tell if any of it helped. I was fixing things in the dark.

And the whole time there was one place I never thought to check.

Something in the back of my mind was already whispering it. I just wasn't ready to hear it.

Then I started remembering things I had been too afraid to connect.

My granddaughter pulling away from me. Not all at once. Slowly. First she stopped sitting in my lap. Then she stopped hugging me. Then she started staying on the other side of the room.

I told myself she was just growing up. Kids do that.

But then I thought about my son. Last time he hugged me at the door, he held his breath. I felt his chest lock up against mine. Just for a second. He thought I wouldn't notice. But when you lose your smell, you start feeling things other people miss. Your whole body pays attention in ways it never did before. I felt him stop breathing.

After the hug he opened both windows in the guest room. It was November.

Then I thought about my neighbor. Every Tuesday we have coffee. And every Tuesday for six months her chair moved a little further from mine. One week she said let's sit outside. It was 45 degrees.

Then my book club. How Carol opens a window when I arrive. How Janet switched seats last month. How nobody says a word but something shifts every time I walk in.

Nobody told me. Not one person. But every single one of them did something.

Standing alone in my hallway at 1 AM, all of it hit me at once. The windows. The chairs. The held breath. The distance. My granddaughter's words.

They could all smell something I couldn't.

It was never the pipes. Never mold. Never the house.

It might be me.

That thought almost broke me.

I stopped inviting people over. Birthdays became phone calls. I quit book club. I couldn't sit in Carol's living room for two hours wondering if everyone was waiting for me to leave.

You want to know the loneliest feeling in the world? Sitting in your own living room afraid to answer the door because you have no idea what hits people when they walk in. And you can't fix it because you can't smell it. And you can't ask because you're terrified of the answer.

I showered twice a day. Bought the most expensive body wash I could find. Scrubbed until my skin turned red. Stayed up past 2 AM searching things I was ashamed to type. "Why do old people smell." "Can you stink and not know it." Found women my age asking the same questions. All of them doing everything right. Not one had figured it out.

I closed my laptop and sat in the dark. This is my life now. A grandmother who makes her own granddaughter sick. And I can't even smell why.

Then Margaret showed up.

body.text:
After my divorce my best friends lied about excluding me from Italy. But they missed my ex-husband more. So I booked the flight and took care of that.

Cassie and I have been best friends for 20 years.

She and Greg. Mike and Pam. Dave and Rachel. Three couples, plus Mark and me.

Every September for 16 years, the 8 of us traveled together.

I researched the towns. I found the excursions. I booked the restaurants. Mark handled the logistics.

For 16 years this was the best week of my year.

Then Mark and I divorced. 14 months ago. He'd been having an affair with a woman from his gym. She was 34.

After the papers were signed, the calls came constantly.

Cassie checking in.

Pam dropping off wine.

Everyone saying "we're here for you, whatever you need."

By month three, the calls slowed down.

By month six, they stopped.

Then I open Instagram on a Tuesday morning. And there they are. All six of them.

At a café in Florence. Cassie's holding a glass of wine and grinning. The caption: "The crew does Italy! 🇮🇹✈️"

The crew.

Without me.

I called Cassie that afternoon.

"Oh, Susan." That voice. The one that sounds like warmth but lands like a verdict.

"We didn't want to make things awkward. It was sort of last-minute. And honestly, sweetheart, we thought you needed a little time for yourself. After everything you've been going through."

Everything I've been going through.

She kept going.

"And it's close quarters over there. One apartment, six of us, the heat in August. Ever since the divorce you just haven't been yourself, Susan."

I sat there and listened.

"It was for your own good. We didn't want you to be overwhelmed."

Two weeks later, they're all back. Tanned. Full of stories.

And Cassie calls me.

"Susan, I have exciting news. We're doing Amalfi in September. And we'd love for you to help plan the itinerary. You always find those incredible hidden restaurants and those excursions nobody else knows about. You're so good at organizing."

I said, "Sure, Cassie. I'll put something together."

Then I hung up. I sat in the kitchen for an hour.

Why did I say yes.

That's the part I kept going back to. She left me off a trip, then called me to plan the next one. And I said sure. Like it was nothing.

Maybe I was being unfair to her. It really could have been last minute. Cassie has not been cruel to me one day in 20 years.

Or maybe I said yes because it was the only thing they still wanted me for.

I sat there a while longer. Then I got the laptop.

I started planning it. Spent weeks on it.

Found a private lemon grove tour on the Amalfi Coast that wasn't in any guidebook.

Booked a sunset dinner reservation at a cliffside restaurant in Positano with a three-month waitlist.

Mapped out walking routes through the terraces that avoided the tourist crush.

Sent it all to the group chat.

Cassie replied: "Susan, this is INCREDIBLE. You're amazing. This is going to be the best one yet!! 💕"

A week later, Cassie invited me to dinner at her house. "Just a little get-together," she said. "Nothing fancy."

I showed up at six.

The good china was out. Candles lit. All three couples were already seated.

They were exchanging looks when I walked in. The kind where everyone knows something you don't.

I thought someone was sick.

After dinner, Cassie cleared her throat.

"Susan, we need to talk about September."

My stomach dropped.

"We've been talking, all of us, and we think it would be better if Mark and Brittany took your spot this year."

Mark.

And Brittany.

The woman he left me for. She was 34. She'd been in his life for two years, one of them while he was still married to me.

"Mark reached out," Cassie continued. "He and Brittany just got engaged. And honestly, we've all known Mark for 20 years. It felt wrong to exclude him forever."

Exclude him.

The man who cheated on me for a year. Who left me for a woman half my age. Who kept the house in the settlement because I couldn't afford to fight him for it.

He's the one they were worried about excluding.

"Susan, we love you. You know that. But nothing has changed since we talked on the phone."

Close quarters. The heat. I just hadn't been myself.

She looked around the table. Like she was checking that everyone still agreed.

They did.

"We just think it's better this way. You have to understand."

You have to understand.

I looked at Cassie. At this woman whose cliffside dinner reservation in Positano I'd spent forty-five minutes on hold to get. Whose lemon grove tour I'd found in a blog written in Italian that I ran through Google Translate three times.

I picked up my wine glass. Took a sip.

"I understand," I said.

I drove home.

I didn't cry. I was past that.

I sat in the kitchen with the lights off.

She wasn't wrong. That was the part I couldn't put down.

The next morning I drove over to Nora's. My sister. 28 years a nurse, most of it on a geriatric floor. She lives 20 minutes away and has never once pretended not to notice something.

I told her everything. The photos from Florence. The "you're so good at organizing" call. The dinner. Cassie's voice. "Ever since the divorce."

And the part I could barely say out loud: that Mark and Brittany were taking my spot. On the trip I planned.

She let me finish. Then she poured the coffee.

She put something on the table between us. Small, wrapped in tissue paper. Orange.

She didn't say a word about it.

"They're right that there's something," she said. "They're wrong about what it is. Those two aren't the same thing."

"Nora, what is this about?"

"28 years I looked after women our age and older. Things change. Your hair goes. Your eyes go. Your skin gets drier."

"Nobody's fault. You color it, you get glasses."

"Well. It also starts making something it never made before. A compound. It has a smell to it. Not a pleasant one."

"I've never heard of that."

"Nobody has. People don't talk about it."

"Then that's not me. I'm a clean person, Nora. I always have been. I buy the good body wash."

"That's the part everybody gets wrong."

She set her cup down.

"Ordinary soap doesn't take it off."

"Now you're being ridiculous."

"Think about garlic. You chop it, then you wash your hands. Twice, with soap. And?"

I didn't answer her.

"And?"

"They still smell."

"They still smell. Your hands are clean and it stayed anyway. Garlic leaves something behind that soap doesn't touch."

"What our skin starts making is called nonenal. Works exactly the same way."

I sat there with that.

"And people notice it," she said. "Not that they know what they're noticing. They couldn't tell you. They just start standing a little further back, and they make up a reason for it afterward."

"Nora."

"You didn't do anything, Susan. Nobody did this to you. Your skin changed at 60 the same way your eyes changed at 45, and nobody sent you a letter about either one."

"So it was never me."

"It was never you."

"Then what gets rid of it?"

She pushed the little parcel across the table.

"I was hoping you'd ask me before I had to offer."

"It's soap. Made from persimmon."

"It doesn't cover it. The tannins take it apart."

"And it works?"

"I sent half my floor home with one. I've used it for years."

"One morning it occurred to me I'd stopped bracing every time somebody hugged me. I never knew I'd been doing it."

I picked it up and held it to my face. Citrus. Warm, though. Not the sharp kind.

"It's called Kaori. I'm down to two bars myself."

I was at the door when she said the other thing.

"Book the flight, Susan. Go on your own."

"Cassie isn't going to un-invite Brittany."

"I'm not talking about Cassie. You found that grove because you wanted to see a grove. You got that table because you wanted to sit at it."

She held the door open.

"So go sit at it."

I drove home with it in my purse.

I used it that night. It's a bar of soap. I didn't expect anything.

The next morning I caught myself standing at the mirror longer than usual. Not for any reason. Just standing. Looking taller, somehow. Skin felt different. Lighter.

I had not stood like that in over a year.

That afternoon I ordered two more. Then I booked the trip.

Same week. Same coast.

Their hotel. One floor up.

Paid for with the money from my half of the retirement account. The only thing I got in the divorce that was actually mine.

And I told no one.

September on the Amalfi Coast is hotter than people think.

I was on the hotel terrace with a glass of prosecco when I saw them come up from the road below. Cassie fanning herself with a folded map. Brittany walking ten feet behind Mark, not talking.

Twenty minutes later Cassie appeared on the terrace. Flushed. Hair coming undone.

She froze.

"Susan? What are you doing here?"

"Same week. Same coast."

She stared a second too long. Then she went to her room without saying anything else.

I didn't move. I had nowhere to be. And a very good glass of prosecco.

Day three. The lemon grove.

Twelve spots. I'd booked one for myself. The group had the rest, because I'd put it in their itinerary.

I got there first. Signora Rossi walked me up through the terraces and showed me how they wrap the lemons in cloth for the winter.

Twenty minutes later, the group arrived.

Signora Rossi looked up and waved at me across the terrace.

"Susan. You are the one who wrote to me. In Italian."

The whole group turned around.

Mark saw me. He stopped.

"Susan? You're on this tour?"

"I found this tour, Mark."

He opened his mouth. Closed it. Looked at Brittany.

Brittany adjusted her sunglasses and said nothing.

There was a woman on the tour with her daughter. About my age. She ended up next to me at the wall while Signora Rossi was talking.

She leaned in slightly. Then leaned back.

"I'm sorry," she said. "Are you wearing something? I've been trying to place it since the van."

"It's a soap."

"It smells so good. Like citrus. Fresh." She laughed at herself. "Sorry. I've been behind you for twenty minutes trying to work out what it was."

"It's called Kaori."

She typed it into her phone right there against the wall.

Cassie was three feet away with her hand cupped over her eyes against the sun.

She didn't say anything.

I thought about that on the walk back down.

We've been talking, all of us. That is what Cassie said at the table.

All of them. Talking. And not one of them ever talked to me.

I think I understood now.

That evening the group was at the bar on the hotel terrace. I was two tables away with a book.

Dave came over. The quietest of the husbands. He sat on the edge of the chair next to mine.

"You planned every good thing that's happened on this trip," he said. "And you're the one who wasn't supposed to be here."

He looked back toward the bar. Then he got up and went back to it.

I didn't read another page.

Night four. The dinner Cassie had booked for the group.

I came down at eight.

Cassie was already seated, fanning herself with the menu. Brittany's shoulders were burned across the top. She kept shifting in her chair.

Mark looked up when I walked in.

After the first course, a woman at the next table leaned over.

Mid-50s. Elegant. Small leather journal next to her plate, pen clipped to it.

"Excuse me," she said. "I'm sorry to interrupt. But I have to ask what you're wearing."

"It's a soap."

"A soap." She put her hand on her chest. "I write for a travel magazine. I've been trying to place that since you sat down. It isn't perfume. It's citrus, and it's fresh. It's lovely."

"Kaori. My sister gave it to me."

"Can I get it here?"

"They only make it when the persimmons come in," I said. "Once a year."

She wrote it in the journal anyway.

Brittany leaned over and said something to Mark. He didn't answer her.

Cassie watched all of it.

The woman with the journal. The pen.

She picked up her wine glass. Took a long sip. Set it down. Looked straight ahead.

Brittany had stopped shifting in her chair.

Mark was watching me. Not Brittany. Me.

Day seven I ate alone at the cliffside table in Positano. The one I'd booked three months earlier, for them.

They had tried for it that morning. Fully booked, the restaurant told them.

Last night. Farewell dinner.

Cassie found me on the terrace afterward. Water black. Stars everywhere.

She sat down.

We were quiet for a while.

"Greg hasn't left the room with the air conditioning since Tuesday," she said.

"That's a shame."

"Brittany's shoulders are blistering. She had to wear a shawl to dinner."

"I noticed."

She looked at me.

"People keep asking about you."

"They do."

"The woman with the journal. The girl at the front desk asked me what my friend uses."

Silence.

"Where did you get it?"

I looked at her.

"Kaori," I said. "But they only make it when the persimmons come in. That batch is gone."

She looked down.

"Of course it is."

"They restock when the fruit comes in. If you wait, you wait a long time."

She nodded.

I stood up.

"Safe travels home, Cassie."

I walked back to my room without looking back.

Here's what I keep coming back to.

They left me off a trip, then called me to plan the next one. Apparently I'm capable enough to find a restaurant with a three-month waitlist. Just not capable enough to sit at one.

"We thought you needed a little time for yourself."

"Ever since the divorce, you just haven't been yourself."

Not one of them ever told me what they actually meant.

My sister did. In her kitchen, in about ten minutes.

Nora called last week. Kaori has a new batch up. It's already most of the way gone.

They're doing September again next year. Sicily, someone said.

Nora has already asked whether Sicily has lemon groves.

I told her yes.

If someone has excluded you and then asked you to do the work anyway.

If they've replaced you with someone younger and then handed you the planning.

If they think losing your husband means you lost yourself.

You don't need to be replaced.

You need to be underestimated one more time.

So you can show them exactly who they were wrong about.

Get the Kaori. Run the bath. Go anyway.

It costs less than fifty cents a day. Less than the coffee I drink while I plan other people's trips.

They only make it when the persimmons come in. Once a batch goes, you wait months.

Cassie asked where I got it. I told her it was sold out.

She's waiting until next year.

I was already home.

Your move.

My son used to come by almost every day. He lives fifteen minutes away.

Then one day he just stopped.

And I spent a year blaming myself before I found out why.

His name is Daniel. Thirty-one. Good job, married, has a little girl named Lily who just turned three. I am so proud of him. Of the father he's become. Of everything he's built.

He'd swing by after work three, four times a week. Sometimes just for twenty minutes and a coffee. I loved hearing about his day. What happened at work, who said what, the little things nobody else cares about but your mother does.

Sometimes he'd stay an hour. Fix something in the house, check the smoke detectors, tighten a cabinet door that had been loose for weeks. Not because I asked. Because that's just who he is.

Saturdays were ours.

He'd pull into the driveway around nine, sometimes with Lily in the back seat, let himself in, and I'd already have the coffee going. He'd mow the lawn in summer, rake leaves in fall, clear the gutters before winter. Then we'd cook lunch together.

His spot at the kitchen table. Second chair from the window. His toolbox in my garage, right side, bottom shelf. His mug on the counter, the one with the faded logo from his college that I offered to replace a hundred times but he wouldn't let me.

Five years of that.

Five years of hearing the screen door and knowing it was him before I even looked up.

I'm not some frail old woman sitting in a chair waiting for company. I'm sixty-eight. I go to the farmers market on Thursdays. I walk three miles every morning. I do my own taxes. I have friends. I have a full life.

But Daniel was the best part of it.

So when that started to disappear, I felt it in a way I can't fully describe. Like the house got quieter even when the TV was on. Like the coffee tasted different when you're only making it for one.

It didn't happen overnight.

There was no fight. No argument. No moment I could point to and say that's where it all went wrong.

He just started staying shorter.

The coffee he used to drink sitting down at the table, he started drinking standing up. Near the door. Jacket still on. Like he was already halfway out before he'd even arrived.

I'd ask if he wanted lunch. He'd say he already ate.

He started opening the kitchen window when he came in. Even in October. I thought maybe he was warm from the drive. I didn't think anything of it.

I should have.

Then the weekday visits stopped.

"Busy at work." Sure. Of course. I didn't push.

Then Saturdays got shorter. He stopped bringing Lily.

He'd come alone, do whatever needed doing, and leave before I could even set the table. I started making his favorite, my pot roast, every Saturday morning. The one with the carrots and the potatoes falling apart, the one he's loved since he was nine. Took me all morning. It sat on the stove getting cold more times than I want to admit.

Then he stopped coming at all.

Started sending a handyman instead. For things he could've done in ten minutes with his eyes closed. A leaky faucet. A squeaky hinge.

Those repairs were never about the repair. They were about him walking through my door. And now a stranger was doing it instead.

Then it was just phone calls. Short ones.

"Everything okay, Mom?"

"Yeah."

"Good. Talk soon."

Three sentences. That was my son now. Three sentences and a dial tone.

I went through it every single night. Lying in bed at 11pm, staring at the ceiling, running through every conversation we'd had in the last six months.

Did I say something wrong? Did I overstep with Lily? Did I complain too much about my hip? Was I too needy? Too clingy? Was I just... too much?

I asked my sister. She said what everyone says.

He's a grown man, he has his own life now. He has a wife and a daughter. Boys pull away. It's what they do. It's normal.

But I know my son.

And this wasn't normal. This wasn't pulling away. This was something else. Something with a shape I couldn't see. Something nobody was willing to name.

Then came his birthday. November.

He came for dinner. I'd spent the whole day cooking. Made everything he loves. Set the table properly, the good plates, candles, the works.

He hugged me at the door.

Fast. Head turned to the side. One arm, not two. I felt him hold his breath. Just for a second. Just long enough for me to notice but not long enough to be sure I wasn't imagining it.

At the table he sat at the far end. As far from me as possible.

When I leaned over to pour his wine he shifted back in his chair. Just slightly. Not rude. Almost like a reflex. Like his body was making space his mouth didn't know how to ask for.

He left early. Said he had an early morning.

I stood in the kitchen after the door closed and picked up the cardigan I'd been wearing all evening. Held it to my face.

Wool. Maybe a little kitchen. Nothing.

But I couldn't stop seeing his face. The way he turned when I hugged him. The way he leaned back when I got close. That tiny held breath.

Something was wrong. I just didn't know what it was.

Until Donna told me.

We've known each other twenty-five years. Book club, birthdays, long walks after church. She's the one friend who says the thing everyone else is just thinking.

I was telling her about Daniel. Just the pulling-away part. Not the birthday dinner. Not the held breath. Just that he wasn't coming around much anymore and I couldn't figure out why.

She went quiet.

Not normal quiet. The kind of quiet where you can feel the next sentence before it arrives. The kind where you know whatever comes next is going to rearrange something inside you.

"Can I be honest with you?" she said. "You're not going to like it."

I said yes. My hands were already gripping the armrest.

"It's not about anything you said. It's not about anything you did. It's about how you smell."

I didn't move.

"I've noticed it for a while now. On your clothes. In your car. It's not a hygiene thing. I know you're clean. But there's something there. And I think Daniel can smell it too."

I just sat there looking at her. Twenty-five years of friendship and I had no idea what to say.

I didn't sleep that night.

I kept lifting my wrist to my nose. Smelling my pillow. My sleeve. My collar. Nothing. I couldn't detect anything wrong with any of it.

But Donna doesn't make things up. And she wouldn't have sat on something like that unless she'd been thinking about it for a very long time and finally couldn't hold it in anymore.

So I did what you do at midnight when the person you trust most just told you something you can't unhear.

I opened my laptop and typed "why do I smell different as I get older."

I didn't close it until two in the morning. And what I found changed everything.

There's a compound called 2-nonenal.

Your body starts producing it around forty. By your sixties and seventies it's just there. On your skin. In your clothes. In every room you spend time in.

In Japan they have a word for it. Kareishū. Aging scent. It's not considered embarrassing over there. It's just a thing that happens. Like gray hair. Like needing reading glasses.

But here's what nobody tells you.

Your skin chemistry changes as you age. The oils on your skin start breaking down through oxidation, kind of like how a sliced apple turns brown on the counter. That process produces a smell. Not terrible. But persistent.

It gets into fabric. It fills up closed rooms. It clings to furniture and coats and pillowcases and car seats and the air around you wherever you go.

And here's the part that broke me wide open.

You can't smell it on yourself.

Your nose adjusts to your own scent. Your brain just filters it out. So it's always there. On you, around you, filling your house, hanging in the air between you and the people you love.

And you have absolutely no idea.

But your son does. Your daughter-in-law does. Your granddaughter does. Your neighbor, your friend, the woman at the checkout. Everyone except you.

And nobody says a word.

Because how do you tell your mother she smells old? You don't. You just visit a little less. Call a little shorter. Hug a little faster. Stand a little further back. Stop bringing the grandkids.

And the person it's happening to lies awake at night trying to figure out what she did wrong.

That was me. Every single night at my kitchen table. Wondering what I did. When the answer was on my skin the entire time.

I kept reading. Found a forum for older women where someone had posted about this exact thing. She said she'd developed the smell and was too embarrassed to stand near anyone anymore. Said social distancing actually felt like a relief because at least now she had an excuse.

On a parenting site, a daughter wrote that the smell in her mother's house had gotten into everything. Her hair, her clothes, even plastic. She said it was stopping her family from visiting. And she felt terrible about it.

I read that and my stomach dropped.

Because that was me. I was the mother in that story. Except nobody had told me.

I kept reading. Regular soap doesn't touch nonenal.

Doesn't matter how expensive it is or how good it smells. Nonenal isn't regular body odor. It's not water-soluble. It bonds to your skin differently. Regular soap just slides right past it.

That's why nothing changes no matter how often you shower. That's why perfume doesn't help. You're just layering something on top. The cause is still right there, on your skin, every single day.

I tried everything in that first week. New soap, expensive body wash, extra showers. Nothing worked. Because I didn't understand yet that I was fighting something regular products were never designed to fight.

Then I found the thing that made me stop scrolling.

Japanese persimmon extract. Kakishibu.

The tannins in it grab onto nonenal and break it apart. Don't cover it. Don't mask it. Dissolve it at the source before it ever gets into your clothes, your furniture, the air in your living room.

In Japan this is just normal soap. Older people use it the way we use Dove. It's in every drugstore. Nobody thinks twice about it.

We just don't know about it here. Nobody told us.

I sat at my kitchen table at two in the morning and suddenly everything made sense.

Every. Single. Thing.

The open windows. The jacket he kept on. The coffee in the doorway. The handyman he sent instead of himself. The Saturdays that disappeared. Lily who stopped coming. The pot roast on the stove getting cold. The birthday hug with his head turned away and his breath held for one second too long.

None of it was about me.

None of it was about growing up or being busy or pulling away.

It was one compound. On my skin. In my house. In the air between me and my son. And everyone I loved had been quietly rearranging their lives around it instead of telling me.

I ordered it that week.

The real thing. Actual kakishibu extract. Most soaps don't have it. I looked. There are cheap ones that just slap "persimmon" on the label and hope you don't know the difference. This was the only one I could find with the real tannins, the actual compound that breaks nonenal apart. Not a fragrance. Not a cover-up. The real thing.

Started using it every day. Skin, hair, behind the ears. Washed my cardigans. Changed the pillowcases. Scrubbed the couch covers.

After about ten days I picked up my pillowcase and held it to my face.

Cotton. Just cotton.

The cardigan smelled like wool. The house smelled like nothing. Like air.

I didn't call Daniel. Didn't explain anything. Didn't say "I figured it out" or "please come back." There was nothing to explain. You don't apologize for something your body did without your permission. You just fix it and let the fixing speak for itself.

Two weeks later I heard the screen door.

No phone call first. No text. No reason.

Daniel walked in. Lily was on his arm.

She wiggled down the second she saw me and ran straight into the kitchen.

"Grandma, up!"

I picked her up. She buried her face into my neck and just stayed there. Breathing. Completely relaxed. Like she'd been missing something she was too small to name.

Daniel came in behind her. Took off his jacket. Hung it on the hook by the door.

Sat down at the kitchen table. His spot. Second chair from the window.

"Got any coffee?"

I made coffee. Took his mug out of the cabinet, the one with the faded logo. He wrapped both hands around it and leaned back in his chair. Not away from me. Just comfortable. At ease. Like someone who wasn't counting the minutes until he could leave.

I started on the pot roast because it was almost Saturday anyway and I hadn't cooked it for someone who actually stayed in months.

When his wife came at six he looked up and said "Already?"

Nobody said anything about what had changed. The thing that was wrong was just gone. Daniel was at my table again. Lily was on my hip. The house was full in a way it hadn't been for a year.

When he left he hugged me.

Not the birthday hug. A real one. Both arms. Face against my shoulder.

Breathing in.

He held on for a long time. I counted. Four seconds.

If your son has pulled away. If the visits got shorter. If the phone calls replaced the doorbell. If he stopped bringing the grandkids. If he sent someone else to do what he used to do himself.

It might not be what you think.

It's not about growing up. It's not about being busy or having his own life or not caring.

It might be the one thing no one in your family will ever say to your face.

I lost a year with Daniel over this. A whole year of Saturdays and coffee and pot roast and his toolbox gathering dust in my garage. A year of Lily growing up without flour on her nose in her grandmother's kitchen. A year I will never get back.

Because nobody told me. And I couldn't smell it myself.

If any of this sounds familiar, if you've been lying awake wondering why someone you love pulled away, I'll leave a link below to the one I use.

It's just soap. You use it and the problem goes away.

I wish someone had told me a year ago. So I'm telling you now.

I picked her up. She buried her face into my neck and just stayed there. Breathing. Completely relaxed. Like she'd been missing something she was too small to name.

Daniel came in behind her. Took off his jacket. Hung it on the hook by the door.

Sat down at the kitchen table. His spot. Second chair from the window.

"Got any coffee?"

I made coffee. Took his mug out of the cabinet, the one with the faded logo. He wrapped both hands around it and leaned back in his chair. Not away from me. Just comfortable. At ease. Like someone who wasn't counting the minutes until he could leave.

I started on the pot roast because it was almost Saturday anyway and I hadn't cooked it for someone who actually stayed in months.

When his wife came at six he looked up and said "Already?"

Nobody said anything about what had changed. The thing that was wrong was just gone. Daniel was at my table again. Lily was on my hip. The house was full in a way it hadn't been for a year.

When he left he hugged me.

Not the birthday hug. A real one. Both arms. Face against my shoulder.

Breathing in.

He held on for a long time. I counted. Four seconds.

If your son has pulled away. If the visits got shorter. If the phone calls replaced the doorbell. If he stopped bringing the grandkids. If he sent someone else to do what he used to do himself.

It might not be what you think.

It's not about growing up. It's not about being busy or having his own life or not caring.

It might be the one thing no one in your family will ever say to your face.

I lost a year with Daniel over this. A whole year of Saturdays and coffee and pot roast and his toolbox gathering dust in my garage. A year of Lily growing up without flour on her nose in her grandmother's kitchen. A year I will never get back.

Because nobody told me. And I couldn't smell it myself.

If any of this sounds familiar, if you've been lying awake wondering why someone you love pulled away, I'll leave a link below to the one I use.

It's just soap. You use it and the problem goes away.

I wish someone had told me a year ago. So I'm telling you now.

body.text:
After my divorce my best friends lied about excluding me from Italy. But they missed my ex-husband more. So I booked the flight and took care of that.

Cassie and I have been best friends for 20 years.

She and Greg. Mike and Pam. Dave and Rachel. Three couples, plus Mark and me.

Every September for 16 years, the 8 of us traveled together.

I researched the towns. I found the excursions. I booked the restaurants. Mark handled the logistics.

For 16 years this was the best week of my year.

Then Mark and I divorced. 14 months ago. He'd been having an affair with a woman from his gym. She was 34.

After the papers were signed, the calls came constantly.

Cassie checking in.

Pam dropping off wine.

Everyone saying "we're here for you, whatever you need."

By month three, the calls slowed down.

By month six, they stopped.

Then I open Instagram on a Tuesday morning. And there they are. All six of them.

At a café in Florence. Cassie's holding a glass of wine and grinning. The caption: "The crew does Italy! 🇮🇹✈️"

The crew.

Without me.

I called Cassie that afternoon.

"Oh, Susan." That voice. The one that sounds like warmth but lands like a verdict.

"We didn't want to make things awkward. It was sort of last-minute. And honestly, sweetheart, we thought you needed a little time for yourself. After everything you've been going through."

Everything I've been going through.

She kept going.

"And it's close quarters over there. One apartment, six of us, the heat in August. Ever since the divorce you just haven't been yourself, Susan."

I sat there and listened.

"It was for your own good. We didn't want you to be overwhelmed."

Two weeks later, they're all back. Tanned. Full of stories.

And Cassie calls me.

"Susan, I have exciting news. We're doing Amalfi in September. And we'd love for you to help plan the itinerary. You always find those incredible hidden restaurants and those excursions nobody else knows about. You're so good at organizing."

I said, "Sure, Cassie. I'll put something together."

Then I hung up. I sat in the kitchen for an hour.

Why did I say yes.

That's the part I kept going back to. She left me off a trip, then called me to plan the next one. And I said sure. Like it was nothing.

Maybe I was being unfair to her. It really could have been last minute. Cassie has not been cruel to me one day in 20 years.

Or maybe I said yes because it was the only thing they still wanted me for.

I sat there a while longer. Then I got the laptop.

I started planning it. Spent weeks on it.

Found a private lemon grove tour on the Amalfi Coast that wasn't in any guidebook.

Booked a sunset dinner reservation at a cliffside restaurant in Positano with a three-month waitlist.

Mapped out walking routes through the terraces that avoided the tourist crush.

Sent it all to the group chat.

Cassie replied: "Susan, this is INCREDIBLE. You're amazing. This is going to be the best one yet!! 💕"

A week later, Cassie invited me to dinner at her house. "Just a little get-together," she said. "Nothing fancy."

I showed up at six.

The good china was out. Candles lit. All three couples were already seated.

They were exchanging looks when I walked in. The kind where everyone knows something you don't.

I thought someone was sick.

After dinner, Cassie cleared her throat.

"Susan, we need to talk about September."

My stomach dropped.

"We've been talking, all of us, and we think it would be better if Mark and Brittany took your spot this year."

Mark.

And Brittany.

The woman he left me for. She was 34. She'd been in his life for two years, one of them while he was still married to me.

"Mark reached out," Cassie continued. "He and Brittany just got engaged. And honestly, we've all known Mark for 20 years. It felt wrong to exclude him forever."

Exclude him.

The man who cheated on me for a year. Who left me for a woman half my age. Who kept the house in the settlement because I couldn't afford to fight him for it.

He's the one they were worried about excluding.

"Susan, we love you. You know that. But nothing has changed since we talked on the phone."

Close quarters. The heat. I just hadn't been myself.

She looked around the table. Like she was checking that everyone still agreed.

They did.

"We just think it's better this way. You have to understand."

You have to understand.

I looked at Cassie. At this woman whose cliffside dinner reservation in Positano I'd spent forty-five minutes on hold to get. Whose lemon grove tour I'd found in a blog written in Italian that I ran through Google Translate three times.

I picked up my wine glass. Took a sip.

"I understand," I said.

I drove home.

I didn't cry. I was past that.

I sat in the kitchen with the lights off.

She wasn't wrong. That was the part I couldn't put down.

The next morning I drove over to Nora's. My sister. 28 years a nurse, most of it on a geriatric floor. She lives 20 minutes away and has never once pretended not to notice something.

I told her everything. The photos from Florence. The "you're so good at organizing" call. The dinner. Cassie's voice. "Ever since the divorce."

And the part I could barely say out loud: that Mark and Brittany were taking my spot. On the trip I planned.

She let me finish. Then she poured the coffee.

She put something on the table between us. Small, wrapped in tissue paper. Orange.

She didn't say a word about it.

"They're right that there's something," she said. "They're wrong about what it is. Those two aren't the same thing."

"Nora, what is this about?"

"28 years I looked after women our age and older. Things change. Your hair goes. Your eyes go. Your skin gets drier."

"Nobody's fault. You color it, you get glasses."

"Well. It also starts making something it never made before. A compound. It has a smell to it. Not a pleasant one."

"I've never heard of that."

"Nobody has. People don't talk about it."

"Then that's not me. I'm a clean person, Nora. I always have been. I buy the good body wash."

"That's the part everybody gets wrong."

She set her cup down.

"Ordinary soap doesn't take it off."

"Now you're being ridiculous."

"Think about garlic. You chop it, then you wash your hands. Twice, with soap. And?"

I didn't answer her.

"And?"

"They still smell."

"They still smell. Your hands are clean and it stayed anyway. Garlic leaves something behind that soap doesn't touch."

"What our skin starts making is called nonenal. Works exactly the same way."

I sat there with that.

"And people notice it," she said. "Not that they know what they're noticing. They couldn't tell you. They just start standing a little further back, and they make up a reason for it afterward."

"Nora."

"You didn't do anything, Susan. Nobody did this to you. Your skin changed at 60 the same way your eyes changed at 45, and nobody sent you a letter about either one."

"So it was never me."

"It was never you."

"Then what gets rid of it?"

She pushed the little parcel across the table.

"I was hoping you'd ask me before I had to offer."

"It's soap. Made from persimmon."

"It doesn't cover it. The tannins take it apart."

"And it works?"

"I sent half my floor home with one. I've used it for years."

"One morning it occurred to me I'd stopped bracing every time somebody hugged me. I never knew I'd been doing it."

I picked it up and held it to my face. Citrus. Warm, though. Not the sharp kind.

"It's called Kaori. I'm down to two bars myself."

I was at the door when she said the other thing.

"Book the flight, Susan. Go on your own."

"Cassie isn't going to un-invite Brittany."

"I'm not talking about Cassie. You found that grove because you wanted to see a grove. You got that table because you wanted to sit at it."

She held the door open.

"So go sit at it."

I drove home with it in my purse.

I used it that night. It's a bar of soap. I didn't expect anything.

The next morning I caught myself standing at the mirror longer than usual. Not for any reason. Just standing. Looking taller, somehow. Skin felt different. Lighter.

I had not stood like that in over a year.

That afternoon I ordered two more. Then I booked the trip.

Same week. Same coast.

Their hotel. One floor up.

Paid for with the money from my half of the retirement account. The only thing I got in the divorce that was actually mine.

And I told no one.

September on the Amalfi Coast is hotter than people think.

I was on the hotel terrace with a glass of prosecco when I saw them come up from the road below. Cassie fanning herself with a folded map. Brittany walking ten feet behind Mark, not talking.

Twenty minutes later Cassie appeared on the terrace. Flushed. Hair coming undone.

She froze.

"Susan? What are you doing here?"

"Same week. Same coast."

She stared a second too long. Then she went to her room without saying anything else.

I didn't move. I had nowhere to be. And a very good glass of prosecco.

Day three. The lemon grove.

Twelve spots. I'd booked one for myself. The group had the rest, because I'd put it in their itinerary.

I got there first. Signora Rossi walked me up through the terraces and showed me how they wrap the lemons in cloth for the winter.

Twenty minutes later, the group arrived.

Signora Rossi looked up and waved at me across the terrace.

"Susan. You are the one who wrote to me. In Italian."

The whole group turned around.

Mark saw me. He stopped.

"Susan? You're on this tour?"

"I found this tour, Mark."

He opened his mouth. Closed it. Looked at Brittany.

Brittany adjusted her sunglasses and said nothing.

There was a woman on the tour with her daughter. About my age. She ended up next to me at the wall while Signora Rossi was talking.

She leaned in slightly. Then leaned back.

"I'm sorry," she said. "Are you wearing something? I've been trying to place it since the van."

"It's a soap."

"It smells so good. Like citrus. Fresh." She laughed at herself. "Sorry. I've been behind you for twenty minutes trying to work out what it was."

"It's called Kaori."

She typed it into her phone right there against the wall.

Cassie was three feet away with her hand cupped over her eyes against the sun.

She didn't say anything.

I thought about that on the walk back down.

We've been talking, all of us. That is what Cassie said at the table.

All of them. Talking. And not one of them ever talked to me.

I think I understood now.

That evening the group was at the bar on the hotel terrace. I was two tables away with a book.

Dave came over. The quietest of the husbands. He sat on the edge of the chair next to mine.

"You planned every good thing that's happened on this trip," he said. "And you're the one who wasn't supposed to be here."

He looked back toward the bar. Then he got up and went back to it.

I didn't read another page.

Night four. The dinner Cassie had booked for the group.

I came down at eight.

Cassie was already seated, fanning herself with the menu. Brittany's shoulders were burned across the top. She kept shifting in her chair.

Mark looked up when I walked in.

After the first course, a woman at the next table leaned over.

Mid-50s. Elegant. Small leather journal next to her plate, pen clipped to it.

"Excuse me," she said. "I'm sorry to interrupt. But I have to ask what you're wearing."

"It's a soap."

"A soap." She put her hand on her chest. "I write for a travel magazine. I've been trying to place that since you sat down. It isn't perfume. It's citrus, and it's fresh. It's lovely."

"Kaori. My sister gave it to me."

"Can I get it here?"

"They only make it when the persimmons come in," I said. "Once a year."

She wrote it in the journal anyway.

Brittany leaned over and said something to Mark. He didn't answer her.

Cassie watched all of it.

The woman with the journal. The pen.

She picked up her wine glass. Took a long sip. Set it down. Looked straight ahead.

Brittany had stopped shifting in her chair.

Mark was watching me. Not Brittany. Me.

Day seven I ate alone at the cliffside table in Positano. The one I'd booked three months earlier, for them.

They had tried for it that morning. Fully booked, the restaurant told them.

Last night. Farewell dinner.

Cassie found me on the terrace afterward. Water black. Stars everywhere.

She sat down.

We were quiet for a while.

"Greg hasn't left the room with the air conditioning since Tuesday," she said.

"That's a shame."

"Brittany's shoulders are blistering. She had to wear a shawl to dinner."

"I noticed."

She looked at me.

"People keep asking about you."

"They do."

"The woman with the journal. The girl at the front desk asked me what my friend uses."

Silence.

"Where did you get it?"

I looked at her.

"Kaori," I said. "But they only make it when the persimmons come in. That batch is gone."

She looked down.

"Of course it is."

"They restock when the fruit comes in. If you wait, you wait a long time."

She nodded.

I stood up.

"Safe travels home, Cassie."

I walked back to my room without looking back.

Here's what I keep coming back to.

They left me off a trip, then called me to plan the next one. Apparently I'm capable enough to find a restaurant with a three-month waitlist. Just not capable enough to sit at one.

"We thought you needed a little time for yourself."

"Ever since the divorce, you just haven't been yourself."

Not one of them ever told me what they actually meant.

My sister did. In her kitchen, in about ten minutes.

Nora called last week. Kaori has a new batch up. It's already most of the way gone.

They're doing September again next year. Sicily, someone said.

Nora has already asked whether Sicily has lemon groves.

I told her yes.

If someone has excluded you and then asked you to do the work anyway.

If they've replaced you with someone younger and then handed you the planning.

If they think losing your husband means you lost yourself.

You don't need to be replaced.

You need to be underestimated one more time.

So you can show them exactly who they were wrong about.

Get the Kaori. Run the bath. Go anyway.

It costs less than fifty cents a day. Less than the coffee I drink while I plan other people's trips.

They only make it when the persimmons come in. Once a batch goes, you wait months.

Cassie asked where I got it. I told her it was sold out.

She's waiting until next year.

I was already home.

Your move.

cards.body:
My grandson shoved me out of his life after a year of college. He was everything to me. I didn't know why until it was almost too late.

I changed that boy's diapers. I taught him how to hold a fishing rod down at the creek when he was so small the rod was taller than him.

Every Friday night for years he'd sleep over at my house. Board games until he fell asleep on the couch.

I'd carry him to bed and he'd wrap his little arms around my neck so tight I could barely breathe.

He never wanted to let go.

When Harold passed two years ago, my grandson drove over and sat with me on the porch for three hours. Didn't say a word. Just sat there while I cried.

That's my boy.

He's twenty now. But he's still my baby.

So when he went off to college I told myself: eleven months. He'll be home. We'll sit on that porch again and it'll be like nothing changed.

I had his favorite dinner ready the day he came home. Pot roast. Carrots the way he likes. Potatoes crispy on the edges.

Set the table for two. Put out the good plates.

Picked him up at the airport. Stood at that gate like it was Christmas morning. Opened my arms because that's what you do when your whole heart is walking toward you.

He hugged me. But it was quick. One arm. Head turned. And he pulled back before I was ready to let go.

I told myself it was the airport. Boys that age don't do big hugs with their grandma in public. That's what I told myself.


The car ride home was quiet. I kept talking. The pot roast, the neighbors, church. He gave me one-word answers and kept his window cracked even though it was cold out.

He said he was tired. Wanted to drop his stuff at his mom's first.

"I'll come by later, Meemaaw."

He didn't come by later.

I called the next morning. He said maybe. Maybe turned into "I told Kyle I'd hang out." That turned into three days of nothing.

When he finally stopped by he stayed forty minutes.

Sat on the edge of the couch. Not sunk into it the way he used to. On the edge. Like he was counting the minutes.

And when he left, there it was again. That hug. Quick. One arm. Head turned.

Something was very wrong. And I had no idea what.


I went through it every night. Lying in bed. Harold's side cold and empty.

What did I do wrong?

Is my house just too boring? No good WiFi. No big TV. Just Harold's chair and my puzzles and a seventy-four-year-old woman who thinks pot roast is still enough.

Maybe I'm not enough anymore.

I called my daughter. Tried to sound casual. Not like I'd been crying into a dish towel every night for two weeks.

"Mom. He's twenty. Kids get independent. It's normal."

But it didn't feel normal. Normal is slow. Normal is calling a little less.

This felt like a door got shut while I was still standing in the doorway.


Then I started noticing things that had nothing to do with my grandson.

The woman at the farmer's market who always hugged me hello. Then one Saturday she just waved from a few feet away.

My friend Patty at book club. Turning her head when I leaned in to talk.

The checkout girl at Kroger. Leaning back when I handed her my coupons.

Once you see it, you can't stop seeing it.

And nobody says anything. Ever.

They'll step back and smile. They'll wave instead of hug. They'll say "he's just at that age."

Because that's easier than saying what they're really thinking.

You walk around every day and you just don't know.

Unless somebody loves you enough to say it.


My daughter did.

I called her again. Three weeks after the airport. This time I didn't play casual.

She went quiet. Real quiet.

"Mom. Please don't take this the wrong way."

My stomach dropped.

"There's a smell. It's not like you're not clean, Mom. It's just... it's gotten worse. And I think that's why he doesn't stay long."

I sat down right there on the kitchen floor. Seventy-four years old. On the linoleum Harold put down himself.

"That's impossible. I shower every day. I use soap. I would KNOW."

She just said: "I know, Mom."


Next morning I scrubbed with new soap from the pharmacy. The expensive kind. Fresh clothes. Perfume.

I thought: okay. Fixed it.

Except a few hours later I hugged my daughter and I watched her face. She tried to hide it. But I saw it.

Nothing had changed.

If soap and water could fix this, it never would have gotten this bad. I shower every day. I always have.

So why wasn't it working?


I called my friend Linda. Ten at night. She worked in a nursing home for over a decade. Bathed people. Sat with families. She doesn't sugarcoat.

I told her everything.

She wasn't surprised.

"Honey," she said. "It's something called Nonenal."

She told me our skin changes as we get older. Starting around forty, the body makes more of a certain oil. When it breaks down on the skin, it turns into this stuff called Nonenal.

Smells stale. Musty. Greasy. Not like sweat. Something else entirely.

And you can't smell it on yourself.

Your nose gets used to your own scent. So it builds and builds and you have no idea.

"So I'll shower more," I said. "Stronger soap."

"That won't work."

"Why not?"

"Think about grease on a pan. You can run hot water over it all day. Scrub it with dish soap. But that greasy film stays right there until you use something that actually cuts through it.

Nonenal is like that. It sits on your skin. Regular soap just slides right over it.

You could shower five times a day and it won't make one bit of difference."

I just sat there.

"That's why nobody figures it out. They shower more. Buy fancier soap. Spray perfume. And nothing changes.

Because the thing causing the smell is still sitting right there on their skin."


"So what do I do?"

She told me about persimmon. Not the fruit. The extract.

In Japan, they've known about this forever. Over there it's not shameful. It's just something you take care of. Like brushing your teeth.

They make soap with persimmon because the tannins in it grab onto Nonenal and break it apart.

That's the only thing that does.

"Over here," Linda said, "nobody even tells you this is a thing. No doctor. No magazine. Nobody.

We just spray perfume on top of it like putting air freshener in a room with a gas leak.

Over there they fixed it. Decades ago."

I asked if she used it.

"You think I spent eleven years in a nursing home and didn't learn a thing? Of course I use it.

I'd rather use a soap that works than watch people lean away from me and pretend they didn't."

She warned me though. Most stuff online that says "persimmon" is junk. Tiny drop buried at the bottom of the ingredients.

She tried three or four before she found one that was real. A brand called Kaori. Actual soap. Real persimmon concentration. Not a body wash pretending to be something it's not.


I ordered it at midnight. Didn't tell a soul.

I felt like a fool. Seventy-four years old, ordering soap off the internet. I thought: this is how they sell things to scared old women.

But then I thought about my boy. Five years old. Running at me so hard he almost knocked me down. Burying his face in my neck and saying "I love you Meemaaw."

And now he can't hug me without turning his head.


First time I used it, I noticed nothing. Of course I didn't. I couldn't smell it before.

But the next time my grandson came by, something shifted.

He sat back on the couch. Not on the edge.

He stayed two hours. We watched one of his movies and I asked too many questions and he laughed at me.

He laughed. In my living room. Like he used to.

And when he left, he hugged me. Not the quick one. Both arms. His chin on top of my head because he's so tall now.

He didn't turn his head.

I closed my eyes and held my boy.


That was four months ago.

He comes by on Sundays now. Sometimes with laundry. Sometimes just to sit.

Last week he fell asleep on the couch and I put a blanket over him and stood there crying like a fool.

Because I got him back.


Look, grandkids grow up. Of course they do. They get busy. They call less. That's life.

But if they really love you, they don't just shove you out for no reason.

My grandson didn't do anything wrong. He just didn't know how to tell his Meemaaw that something was off. And I didn't know it was happening.

That's nobody's fault. But it's something you can fix once you know.

We almost lost each other. Over something I didn't even know was there. Something nobody would say. Something no amount of showering could touch.

If you've got that quiet ache where someone you love is pulling away and everybody tells you it's normal...

Maybe it's not.

Maybe it's the one thing nobody has the heart to tell you.

I wish someone had told me sooner. So I'm telling you now.

I left the link below. This is the thing that helped me get my grandson back and I don't want anyone else to go through what I went through.

They did run out when I first ordered. Small maker. Not some big factory. So I bought extra after that. If I were you I'd do the same.
